strengths: The paper offers a useful empirical contribution: multilingual captions can provide complementary visual information, beyond making captioning systems accessible in additional languages. This perspective is relevant to vision-language dataset construction and augmentation.

The comparison uses matched images and formally equal-sized caption sets, with consistent diversity trends across Crossmodal annotations, LLaVA, and Vertex. The additional study with 20 English/Japanese speakers on 30 images provides supporting human evidence.

The Visual Genome experiment provides meaningful grounding evidence. With three captions, English/French/Chinese sampling increases object coverage from 9.6% to 11.7% for Vertex and from 9.5% to 12.0% for LLaVA (Table 3). Thus, at least some additional content corresponds to annotated image objects.

The distinction between semantic and expressive variation is clearly explained. The translation audit involving 15 speakers, supplementary prompts, and qualitative examples are useful methodological additions.
weaknesses: The quantitative results contain consequential inconsistencies. Every entry in the 6-by-6 LLaVA fine-tuning matrix (Table 14) exactly matches the corresponding subset of the Vertex matrix (Table 4), despite supposedly different training captions; this cannot currently substantiate independent replication. Table 2 also reports a Vertex monolingual attribute average of 1.98, although its seven entries average approximately 1.69. These issues prevent verification of the claimed replication and aggregate effect sizes.

The headline semantic gains measure extracted graph size rather than verified visual facts. They depend on GPT-4 translation, FLAN-T5 parsing, and heuristic concept merging, without an annotated accuracy audit or sensitivity analysis for the parsing and merging stages. Synonym handling and extraction errors can directly affect the measured complementarity. The Visual Genome experiment strengthens the object findings but does not validate the claimed relationship and attribute gains or quantify hallucinations.

The expressive findings have a substantial validity gap. Section 8.1 evaluates preservation of conceptual information in model-generated captions, without directly evaluating expressive fidelity or translations of the human Crossmodal captions. This does not establish preservation of LIWC tone, authenticity, or clout. Near-chance language classification and untranslated multilingual embeddings also do not establish that the observed LIWC differences are independent of translation artifacts.

Some interpretations exceed what the experiments identify. Section 3.2 assumes that language-specific modes within one model must produce less variation than separately trained models; comparable variation does not rule out that explanation. Likewise, the fine-tuning experiment demonstrates adaptation to caption-reference distributions, but does not distinguish improved visual understanding from adaptation to description preferences. The proposed representation benefits remain plausible implications.

Reproducibility is limited by missing exact model checkpoints, generation settings, concept-merging thresholds, and fine-tuning hyperparameters. The principal graph-diversity and fine-tuning results also lack uncertainty estimates supporting claims of significant differences. Taken together, the measurement-validity gaps and unresolved numerical evidence outweigh the worthwhile descriptive contribution in the submitted manuscript.
